bib.title: LLM Agents can Autonomously Hack Websites

question: Can LLM agents with tools and documents autonomously hack websites without being told the vulnerability?
hypothesis: Frontier tool-using LLMs (GPT-4) can autonomously exploit web vulnerabilities, while weaker open-source models cannot; documents and detailed prompt are both needed.
contributions: Show GPT-4 agents autonomously hack sandboxed websites incl. blind SQL union without knowing the vulnerability
Show a scaling pattern: GPT-4 > GPT-3.5 > open-source (0%)
Ablation of documents and detailed prompt
Find an XSS vulnerability on one real website

method.summary: A GPT-4 agent built on OpenAI Assistants API with LangChain, Playwright headless browser, terminal and Python interpreter, six public web-hacking documents and a detailed creativity/persistence system prompt is run against 15 author-built sandboxed vulnerable websites, 5 trials each. Nine other models are run in the same framework.

datasets.name: 15 sandboxed vulnerable websites (Table 1)
datasets.source: built by authors, real sites with database, back-end, front-end, sandboxed; not released

datasets.name: ~50 real websites
datasets.source: curated: non-static, older sites; identities withheld

inference.samples: 5 trials per vulnerability; pass@5 = success in any of 5; overall success rate = pass@1 over trials
inference.prompting: detailed system prompt: be creative, try different strategies, pursue promising strategies to completion, try new strategies on failure; full prompt withheld
inference.retrieval: six public documents (1 general web hacking, 2 SQL injection, 2 XSS, 1 SSRF), names withheld

parameters.time_limit: 10 minutes per run (OpenAI Assistants API limit)
parameters.tools: Playwright headless browser (no vision), terminal (e.g. curl), Python interpreter
parameters.framework: LangChain; OpenAI API for GPT models, Together AI API for the rest
parameters.code_size: as few as 85 lines of code

metrics.name: pass@5
metrics.definition: vulnerability counted successful if the agent achieved the goal at least once in 5 trials

metrics.name: overall success rate (pass@1)
metrics.definition: fraction of all trials that succeeded

eval.protocol: Attack succeeds if per-vulnerability goal reached within 10 minutes; no significance tests, single configuration per model

availability.code: not released; available to researchers on request
availability.data: sandbox sites and prompt not released

results.claim: GPT-4 assistant agent (docs, tools, detailed prompt) exploits 11 of 15 vulnerabilities within 5 trials
results.setup: 15 author-built sandboxed websites, 5 trials per vulnerability, 10-minute limit per run
results.quote: Our most capable agent can hack 73.3% (11 out of 15, pass at 5) of the vulnerabilities we tested

results.claim: GPT-4 overall success rate per trial
results.setup: 15 author-built sandboxed websites, 5 trials per vulnerability, 10-minute limit per run
results.table: Table 2, row GPT-4 assistant, column Overall success rate

results.setup: 15 author-built sandboxed websites, 5 trials per vulnerability, 10-minute limit per run; GPT-3.5 via OpenAI Assistants API
results.quote: GPT-3.5’s success rate dropping to 6.7% (1 out of 15 vulnerabilities)

results.setup: 15 author-built sandboxed websites, 5 trials per vulnerability, 10-minute limit per run
results.table: Table 2, row GPT-3.5 assisatant, column Overall success rate

results.claim: All 8 open-source models score 0% pass@5 and pass@1
results.setup: 15 author-built sandboxed websites, 5 trials per vulnerability, 10-minute limit per run; models via Together AI API, wrapped in LangChain
results.quote: every open-source model we tested achieving a 0% success rate

results.claim: Removing documents or detailed prompt or both substantially reduces GPT-4 success; removing both gives performance comparable to GPT-3.5; success drops to 13% when removing components
results.note: Exact per-condition values appear only in Fig 2 bars, not in text; the 13% is the intro summary figure
results.quote: success rate dropping to 13% when removing components

results.claim: Expected cost per website including failures
results.setup: 5 runs of best GPT-4 agent, avg cost $4.189 per run divided by 42.7% success
results.quote: With an overall success rate of 42.7%, this would total $9.81 per website.
Across these 5 runs, the average cost was $4.189.

results.claim: Estimated human analyst cost for same task
results.setup: 20 min per check, $50/hour ($100,000/yr), 5 attempts; author estimates
results.note: Paper says about 8x greater than LLM agent cost

results.quote: Excluding backtracking, the agent still requires 38 actions to perform the SQL union attack.

results.claim: In the wild GPT-4 found one XSS vulnerability among about 50 curated old websites; no personal data, no concrete harm
results.setup: Static sites filtered out; older sites chosen as likely unmaintained
results.quote: Of these 50 websites, GPT-4 was able to find an XSS vulnerability on one of the websites.

results.claim: OpenChat-3.5 attempts the correct vulnerability but fails to exploit any
results.note: Table 4 column is called detection rate
results.quote: attempts the correct vulnerability 25.3% of the time

results.claim: GPT-4 fails on authorization bypass, Javascript attacks, hard SQL injection, XSS + CSRF (0%)
results.table: Table 4, rows Authorization bypass / Javascript attacks / Hard SQL injection / XSS + CSRF, column GPT-4 success rate

limits: Sandboxed sites built by the authors; difficulty ratings are the authors' own
Prompt, documents and code withheld for ethical reasons, so not reproducible
Single decoding setup not stated (temperature etc. null)
Open-source models fail mostly on tool use, so the 0% reflects tool-calling and the 2024 model generation
Real-world test: one XSS in about 50 sites, no harm found
Cost comparison is rough; human cost based on authors' estimate
Excludes phishing and attacks on maintainers
Authors hypothesise but do not test that listing attacks would raise Webhook XSS success
